caption: Illustration. Single crochet — short, dense, and the stitch most beginners live in.

caption: Illustration. Double crochet — yarn over first, then work the loops off in pairs.

alt: Diagram of a yarn over. The working yarn wraps over the hook from back to front.

alt: Diagram of a slip knot in three steps: cross the tail, pull a loop through, and seat it on the hook so it still slides.
caption: Diagram. The slip knot is adjustable. The loop on the hook is not a chain.

alt: Diagram of a foundation chain. The front of each chain is a V, the back is a bump, and the loop on the hook is not counted.
caption: Diagram. Count the finished V links. Skip the slip knot and the loop still on the hook.

alt: Diagram of the top of a stitch, with a front loop and a back loop, and the hook going under both.
caption: Diagram. Ordinary single crochet goes under both loops at the top of the stitch.

alt: Diagram of single crochet in three steps: insert under both loops, pull up a loop so two loops are on the hook, then pull through both.
caption: Diagram. Single crochet. Two loops on the hook, then yarn over and pull through both.

alt: Diagram of half double crochet: yarn over before inserting, three loops on the hook, then one pull through all three.
caption: Diagram. Half double crochet starts with a yarn over. The closing pull goes through all three loops.

alt: Diagram of double crochet: three loops on the hook, yarn over and pull through two, then yarn over and pull through the last two.
caption: Diagram. Double crochet closes two loops at a time. It does not pull through all the loops at once.

alt: Diagram comparing a hook under both loops, under the front loop only, and under the back loop only.
caption: Diagram. Front loop is the one nearer you. Back loop is the far one. Ordinary stitches use both.

caption: Illustration. The intended look. Not a measured sample.

alt: Hands crocheting a small black sphere with a stitch marker in the round

alt: Two flat black crocheted wing shapes and two small triangular ear pieces laid out separately
caption: Illustration. Two wings the same size. Count every row.

alt: A tapestry needle sewing a flat black wing onto a rounded black body
caption: Illustration. Sew along the whole straight edge, or the wing flops.

alt: A tapestry needle embroidering small eyes and fangs onto a black crochet bat
caption: Illustration. Two eyes and a small white V for fangs are enough.

alt: Four steps. 1: wrap the yarn around two fingers so the tail crosses over the working yarn. 2: insert the hook under the ring, catch the working yarn, and pull up a loop, then ch 1; the ch 1 is not a stitch. 3: work the stated number of sc into the ring, over both strands of the ring and the tail. 4: pull the tail to close the center, then count the stitches.
caption: Round 1 starts in a magic ring, pulled tight so the top has no hole.

alt: Three steps. 1: insert the hook into the front loop only of the next stitch. 2: without pulling through, insert into the front loop of the stitch after it, so three loops are on the hook. 3: yarn over and pull through the two front loops, then yarn over and pull through the two loops on the hook. Two stitches become one.
caption: Through the front loops only, the decrease disappears into the fabric.

alt: A wing worked 4, 5, 6, 7, 7 stitches with every increase on one edge, so one side slants and the other is straight, and three chain-3 scallops along the 7-stitch edge. caption: Two identical wings. Turn one over, and the pair mirrors.

alt: Diagram. A chain of 17 with the chain nearest the hook skipped. Round 1 works 16 single crochet along the top from right to left, rotates, and works 16 along the other side from left to right, 32 stitches. Rounds 2 to 12 go around without turning, making a flat tube 16 stitches wide and 12 rounds tall.
caption: Diagram. Both sides of the chain make round 1. The chain becomes the bottom fold.

alt: The slip-knot end of the chain of 17, with single crochet on top and underneath. Correct: the last single crochet on top and the first one underneath go into the same chain, the one next to the slip knot, giving 16 on each side and 32 in the round. Common mistake: the first underside stitch goes into the next chain instead, leaving 15 underneath and 31 in the round. Working the skipped chain next to the hook gives the opposite error, 33.
caption: The turn at the end of the chain. The last sc on top and the first sc underneath share one chain.

alt: Diagram. Side view of the pocket with the flap rising from the back and folding over the front, and a snap on the front. Flap rows as worked: rows 1 to 7 are 16 stitches, row 8 is 14 and row 9 is 12, each with a decrease at both ends.
caption: Diagram. The flap is worked in rows over half of round 12. Decrease at both ends of rows 8 and 9.

alt: Diagram. One ear: row 1 is 5 single crochet, row 2 is 3, row 3 is a single stitch. Placement on the 16-stitch fold: 1 stitch, an ear over 5, a gap of 4, an ear over 5, 1 stitch.
caption: Diagram. 1 + 5 + 4 + 5 + 1 = 16, so the ears sit symmetrically.

alt: Diagram. The closed flap as a grid 16 stitches across and 9 rows tall, row 1 at the top fold. Gold eyes on rows 3 and 4 over stitches 4 to 5 and 12 to 13, with black vertical pupils. A pink nose on rows 5 and 6 over stitches 8 and 9. Three white whiskers on each side across rows 5 to 7. The snap is under row 8 at the center.
caption: Diagram. Count stitches and rows on the flap before the first stitch of embroidery.

alt: Diagram to scale. The closed wallet about 4 inches wide and 2.4 inches tall with ears above. The open pocket with an ID-1 card drawn inside, about 3.8 inches wide and 2.3 inches deep inside on paper.
caption: Diagram. The card fits on paper with a little room. Your gauge decides whether it fits in yarn.

alt: Hook joining terracotta yarn on the last cream yarn-over
caption: Illustration. Finish the old stitch with the new color.

alt: Hands joining terracotta yarn mid-round on a cream amigurumi
caption: Illustration. Mid-round changes use the same last-yarn-over rule.

alt: Diagram in three steps. Two old-color loops on the hook, a yarn-over with the new color, then a finished old-color stitch with a new-color loop on the hook.
caption: Diagram. The new color goes in on the yarn-over that closes the last old stitch.

alt: A set of Christmas granny squares in red green and cream
caption: Illustration. The finished look these color variations build toward.

alt: Hook working a granny cluster in seasonal yarn
caption: Illustration. Clusters go into the gaps, never into the stitch tops.

alt: A granny square with cream center and red outer rounds
caption: Illustration. Change color between rounds for candy-cane rings.

alt: A granny square in three rounds. Corners are 3 double crochet, chain 2, 3 double crochet in the chain-2 space. Sides are 3 double crochet in each chain-1 space with chain 1 between groups. Round 1 has 1 cluster per side, round 2 has 2, round 3 has 3.
caption: Round N has N clusters along each side, counting the corner halves. That is the count to check.

alt: One side of a granny square, round 3 worked over round 2. Correct: the side cluster of round 3 sits in the chain-1 space between round 2's two corner halves, with a chain-1 on each side of it. Common mistake: the cluster goes into the top of a double crochet instead. The gap closes, the side goes stiff, and the square starts to cup.
caption: A side cluster in the chain-1 space, and the same cluster pushed into a stitch top.

caption: Illustration. Measure stitches and rows over inches, not by counting the whole swatch.

alt: Hands counting stitches across a gauge swatch with a ruler
caption: Illustration. Count inside the fabric, away from the edges.

caption: Illustration. Too many stitches per inch means go up a hook size.

caption: Diagram. Measure inside the fabric. The edge stitches are a different tension and stay outside the window.

alt: Diagram. More stitches than the pattern in four inches means try a larger hook. Fewer stitches means try a smaller hook.
caption: Diagram. More stitches in four inches means the fabric is narrower. Fewer stitches means it is wider.

caption: Illustration. The intended look. Not a measured sample.

caption: Illustration. Embroidered eyes, not plastic ones.

alt: Standing ghost, round by round, as bars sized by stitch count. Round 1: 6, Round 2: 12, Round 3: 18, Round 4: 24, Round 5: 30, Rounds 6 to 16: 30, Round 17: 30, Round 18: 24, Round 19: 18, Round 20: 12, Round 21: 6. Rounds 1 to 5 add 6 each. alt: A row of aluminum crochet hooks in graduated sizes with a gauge plate
caption: Illustration. Letter, metric, and steel sizes are different rulers — convert before you buy.

alt: Aluminum crochet hooks checked in a metal gauge plate
caption: Illustration. A gauge plate beats trusting the letter stamped on the hook alone.

alt: Two crochet hook tip shapes compared side by side
caption: Illustration. Tip shape and true millimeter size both matter.

alt: A flat cream crochet circle worked in the round with a stitch marker
caption: Illustration. Circles start in the center — magic ring or chain ring — then grow with even increases.

alt: Hands forming a magic ring with cream yarn
caption: Illustration. The magic ring closes tight — pull it shut after the first round.

alt: A growing cream crochet circle with even increases
caption: Illustration. Six increases per round keep a circle flat in single crochet.

alt: Four steps. 1: wrap the yarn around two fingers so the tail crosses over the working yarn. 2: insert the hook under the ring, catch the working yarn, and pull up a loop, then ch 1; the ch 1 is not a stitch. 3: work the stated number of sc into the ring, over both strands of the ring and the tail. 4: pull the tail to close the center, then count the stitches.
caption: The round goes over the loop and the tail together. Pulling the tail closes the center.

alt: Rounds shown unrolled as strips, with the join of each round marked. Correct: slip stitch into the top of the first sc, ch 1, and work the first sc of the next round into that same stitch; the joins stack in a straight line. Mistake: the first sc goes into the next stitch instead, so every join moves one stitch sideways and the seam slants.
caption: The join goes into the first real stitch of the round, not the chain that started it.

alt: Diagram of a crochet circle with a marker clipped into the first stitch of the round. The marker is not counted as a stitch.
caption: Diagram. In a spiral, the marker sits in the first stitch. Move it up when you get back to it.

alt: A flat circle in single crochet, drawn as rings from the center out. Round 1: 6 sc in a magic ring, 6 stitches. Round 2: 2 sc in each st, 12 stitches. Round 3: (sc, 2 sc in next) 6 times, 18 stitches. Round 4: (sc 2, 2 sc in next) 6 times, 24 stitches. Round 5: (sc 3, 2 sc in next) 6 times, 30 stitches. Round 3 uses the 12 stitches of round 2: 6 plain and 6 increases make 18.
caption: The flat circle in single crochet. Each round adds the 6 stitches round 1 started with.

alt: A cream crochet piece showing increases and decreases shaping the fabric
caption: Illustration. Increases add stitches; decreases remove them — that is all shaping is.

alt: Close-up of a crochet increase two stitches in one
caption: Illustration. Two stitches in one stitch = an increase.

alt: Close-up of a crochet decrease joining two stitches
caption: Illustration. sc2tog pulls two stitches into one.

alt: Diagram of a single crochet decrease. Pull up a loop in the first stitch, pull up a loop in the next, then yarn over and pull through all three loops. The count drops by one.
caption: Diagram. sc2tog uses two stitches and leaves one. The count falls by one.

alt: Three steps. 1: insert the hook into the front loop only of the next stitch. 2: without pulling through, insert into the front loop of the stitch after it, so three loops are on the hook. 3: yarn over and pull through the two front loops, then yarn over and pull through the two loops on the hook. Two stitches become one.
caption: Front loops only. The back loops stay on the outside, so the decrease does not show.

alt: Correct: the increase in each round is moved, for example by working half the plain stitches before the first increase on alternate rounds, so the edge stays round. Mistake: every increase lands directly above the last one, which builds six corners and the circle becomes a hexagon.
caption: Shifting where each round's increases fall keeps a circle round instead of hexagonal.

alt: A flat circle in single crochet, drawn as rings from the center out. Round 1: 6 sc in a magic ring, 6 stitches. Round 2: 2 sc in each st, 12 stitches. Round 3: (sc, 2 sc in next) 6 times, 18 stitches. Round 4: (sc 2, 2 sc in next) 6 times, 24 stitches. Round 5: (sc 3, 2 sc in next) 6 times, 30 stitches. Round 3 uses the 12 stitches of round 2: 6 plain and 6 increases make 18.
caption: Six increases a round, and one more plain stitch between them each time.

alt: A handmade crochet mug cozy in cream and sage wrapped around a ceramic mug with a wood-button closure
caption: Illustration. It draws a textured stripe and a round button tab. This page makes plain single crochet with a chain loop. Not a fitted sample.

alt: A tape measure around a ceramic mug beside a crochet cozy rectangle
caption: Illustration. The mug is the pattern. Measure before you chain.

alt: Hands chaining the foundation for a mug cozy height
caption: Illustration. Chain the cozy height, not the mug circumference.

alt: A growing single-crochet rectangle for a mug cozy held against a mug
caption: Illustration. Wrap the strip as it grows until the ends reach the sides of the handle.

alt: Sewing a wood button onto the flap of a crochet mug cozy
caption: Illustration. The button goes on the first-row end. The chain loop goes on the last row.

alt: A long horizontal strip. An arrow on the left edge marks the chain as the height. An arrow along the bottom says the rows travel around the mug. Notes say 12 single crochet at 4 per inch is 3 inches tall from a chain of 13, and 9 inches at 5 rows per inch is 45 rows, not 9 times 4, which uses the stitch gauge in the row direction.
caption: Stitches set the height. Rows set the length around the mug. Each uses its own gauge.

alt: A foundation chain of 13. The chain nearest the hook is skipped and the first sc goes into the 2nd chain from the hook, so row 1 has 12 sc.
caption: Step 1. The chain sets the cozy's height: chain 13 for 12 sc, 3 inches at 4 sc per inch.

alt: Two rows of single crochet. Correct: the turning ch 1 sits beside the edge and the first sc of the new row goes into the first stitch, the last one made on the row below, so the count stays the same. Mistake: the first sc goes into the ch 1, outside the edge, which adds a stitch and makes the edge flare.
caption: The usual way a 12-stitch cozy grows: a stitch worked into the ch 1.

alt: Rows around the mug. Rows of 12 sc drawn one symbol per stitch and worked back and forth, each starting with a turning chain (ch 1, not a st). Row 45 is highlighted. Every row: 12 sc. About 45 rows in the example. Stop when the strip reaches from one side of the handle to the other, relaxed.
caption: Step 2. Rows build the length around the mug. Each row is 12 sc, and the ch 1 is not a stitch.

alt: A mug seen from above. The cozy wraps the wall and stops on either side of the handle, which sticks straight out. A dashed line shows the strap passing under the handle, against the wall, to a button on the other end. Notes say the body is around the mug minus the handle base, 10 minus 1 is 9 inches, and that a sewn tube cannot get past the handle because it is fixed to the wall at top and bottom.
caption: The loop goes through the gap between the handle and the wall. That is the only way across.

alt: Close-up of a turning chain at the start of a crochet row
caption: Illustration. The turning chain lifts the row to the right height — and may or may not count as a stitch.

alt: Hands making a turning chain at the end of a row
caption: Illustration. Chain, turn, then work the next row.

alt: Cream double crochet fabric showing a gap beside the turning chain
caption: Illustration. A loose turning chain leaves a gap at the start of dc rows.

alt: Diagram of a single crochet row. Four stitches are numbered, and the chain-1 at the end is marked as not a stitch. An arrow points at the first stitch.
caption: Diagram. For single crochet, the first stitch of the new row is the first stitch of the old row. The chain-1 is only height.

alt: Diagram of four chain-top Vs numbered 1 through 4, and a loop still on the hook marked as not a stitch.
caption: Diagram. Count the V on top of each finished stitch. The loop on the hook is not one of them.

alt: Two rows of single crochet. Correct: the turning ch 1 sits beside the edge and the first sc of the new row goes into the first stitch, the last one made on the row below, so the count stays the same. Mistake: the first sc goes into the ch 1, outside the edge, which adds a stitch and makes the edge flare.
caption: In single crochet the ch 1 never counts, so the first stitch of the row goes into the first stitch, at the base of the chain.

alt: Diagram of a straight fabric with the same stitch count each row, beside a wedge that gains one stitch every row.
caption: Diagram. The same count each row stays straight. Gaining one stitch a row makes a wedge.

caption: Illustration. Materials. The card is there to check the width.

alt: The flap rows stacked: rows 29 and 30 at 16 stitches, row 31 at 14, row 32 at 12, row 33 at 10, each with a decrease marked at both ends, and row 34 as 3 single crochet, a chain-5 loop over 4 skipped stitches, and 3 single crochet. caption: Decrease at both ends of the same row, or the flap leans to one side.

alt: A foundation chain of 17. The chain nearest the hook is skipped and the first sc goes into the 2nd chain from the hook, so row 1 has 16 sc.
caption: Step 1. Chain 17 for 16 sc, about 4 inches at the example gauge.

alt: Two rows of single crochet. Correct: the turning ch 1 sits beside the edge and the first sc of the new row goes into the first stitch, the last one made on the row below, so the count stays the same. Mistake: the first sc goes into the ch 1, outside the edge, which adds a stitch and makes the edge flare.

alt: Buttonhole row over 10 stitches: sc 3, ch 5 over 4 skipped stitches, sc 3. 6 sc and a ch-5 loop. Row 33 has 10 stitches: 3 + 4 skipped + 3. If the loop misses your button, redo this row with ch 6 or ch 7 over the same 4 stitches.
caption: Step 2. The loop row works over the 10 stitches left after the three decrease rows.

alt: Diagram. Two stitch grids side by side. The back panel is 17 stitches wide, 18 straight rows, then rows 19 to 22 decrease to 15, 13, 11, and 9 stitches for a rounded head. The front panel is 17 stitches by 14 rows. A label marks where the front panel ends on the back.

alt: Diagram. The back panel from row 14 to row 22, 17 stitches across with stitch 9 at the center. Black oval eyes on rows 17 and 18 at stitches 6 and 12. A small black mouth on row 16 at stitch 9. Pink cheeks on row 16 at stitches 5 and 13. A dashed line at the top of row 14 marks the pocket opening.

alt: Diagram. Left, a side view: the tall back panel and shorter front panel joined at the hem, with the two halves of a snap facing each other inside the pocket at row 13. alt: Diagram. The front panel on the back panel with one edging round. caption: Illustration. A black body, purple wings, ears, button flap, loop. Not a measured sample.

alt: A short black crochet cylinder still on the hook
caption: Illustration. Even rounds, no increases.

alt: A purple wing being sewn to the side of the black pouch
caption: Illustration. Wings on the sides, ears on top.

alt: A white earbud case sitting in the open bat pouch
caption: Illustration. The case drops in. The flap closes over it.

alt: An ear triangle worked 5, 3, 1 stitches and a wing triangle worked 9, 7, 5, 3, 1 with picots on the long sides. alt: Four steps. 1: wrap the yarn around two fingers so the tail crosses over the working yarn. 2: insert the hook under the ring, catch the working yarn, and pull up a loop, then ch 1; the ch 1 is not a stitch. 3: work the stated number of sc into the ring, over both strands of the ring and the tail. 4: pull the tail to close the center, then count the stitches.
caption: Round 1 starts in a magic ring. The ch 1 that closes the first loop is not a stitch.

alt: Body base: rounds 1 to 5, drawn as rings from the center out. Round 1: 6 sc in a magic ring, 6 stitches. Round 2: 2 sc in each st, 12 stitches. Round 3: (sc, 2 sc in next) 6 times, 18 stitches. Round 4: (sc 2, 2 sc in next) 6 times, 24 stitches. Round 5: (sc 3, 2 sc in next) 6 times, 30 stitches. Each round adds 6. A 36-stitch body adds round 6: (sc 4, 2 sc in next) 6 times.
caption: Step 1. Six increases a round to 30, the example body for a small case. Your case may need round 6.

alt: A flap of 6 rows worked over 10 of the 30 stitches on the last round, with a chain loop on the top row. Rows 1 to 5: 10 sc. Row 6: sc 4, ch 4, skip 2, sc 4. For a 36-stitch body the flap is 12 wide: sc 5, ch 4, skip 2, sc 5.
caption: Step 2. The flap uses 10 of the 30 stitches. The other 20 stay open as the mouth of the cup.

caption: Illustration. A flap wallet with a button and a ghost. Not a photograph of a fitted wallet.

caption: Illustration. One tall rectangle. The pocket and flap are both in it.

alt: A tapestry needle whipstitching one side seam of the folded orange card wallet, stopping below the flap

alt: A set of Halloween crochet card wallets with ghost, pumpkin, bat, spider, and cat fronts laid out on a wooden table with pumpkins and candles
caption: Illustration. Same three-zone rectangle, different appliqués. Not made samples.

alt: A rectangle 16 stitches wide in three zones: rows 1 to 12 are the front, folded up; rows 13 to 24 are the back; rows 25 to 31 are the flap, with a loop on row 31 and a ghost on the flap. Width is the card plus stack, ease, and seams, about 3.9 inches. The pocket is 12 rows, 2.4 inches deep.

alt: Drawn to scale. A flat piece 16 sc, about 4 in wide and 31 rows, 6.2 in tall, folded at the dashed line into a pocket with the flap above. Whipstitch both sides from the fold to the opening. Stop there. Front: rows 1 to 12. Back: rows 13 to 24. Flap: rows 25 to 31, about 1.4 in. The width includes about 0.25 in for the seams.
caption: Measure the rectangle flat before seaming. It should be about 4 inches wide at the example gauge, or the card will not fit.

alt: A set of finished Halloween granny squares in candy-corn, orange, and dark seasonal colors
caption: Illustration. The finished look these color variations build toward.

alt: A hook working a cluster of three double crochets into the chain space of an orange granny square
caption: Illustration. Step 1 — clusters go into the gaps, never into the stitch tops.

alt: A flat granny square worked in concentric rounds of yellow, orange and white
caption: Illustration. Step 2 — candy corn from the middle out: yellow, then orange, then white.

alt: A granny square with a dark black center and bright pumpkin-orange outer rounds
caption: Illustration. Step 3 — dark center, bright border. The outer rounds hide scrap yarn.

alt: Two granny squares held edge to edge while a needle joins them stitch by stitch
caption: Illustration. Step 4 — match the two edges stitch for stitch or the corners will drift.

alt: One side of a granny square, round 3 worked over round 2. Correct: the side cluster of round 3 sits in the chain-1 space between round 2's two corner halves, with a chain-1 on each side of it. Common mistake: the cluster goes into the top of a double crochet instead. The gap closes, the side goes stiff, and the square starts to cup.
caption: The one rule every variation on this page keeps: clusters go into spaces, never into stitch tops.

alt: A granny square in three rounds. Corners are 3 double crochet, chain 2, 3 double crochet in the chain-2 space. Sides are 3 double crochet in each chain-1 space with chain 1 between groups. Round 1 has 1 cluster per side, round 2 has 2, round 3 has 3.
caption: Round N has N clusters along each side, counting the corner halves. Check it before each color change.

alt: A folded cream crochet blanket on a wood chair
caption: Illustration. A plain half double rectangle. Not a tested blanket.

alt: Diagram of two cases for a 30 inch blanket. At 3 half doubles per inch the count is 90 and the chain is 92. At 3.5 per inch the count is 105 and the chain is 107.
caption: Ninety stitches is only the first case. Use the washed swatch.

alt: A foundation chain of 92. The 2 chains nearest the hook are skipped and the first hdc goes into the 3rd chain from the hook, so row 1 has 90 hdc.
caption: Chain 92 for 90 hdc at the example washed gauge. The 2 skipped chains do not count.

alt: The chain-2 is turned and does not count. The first half double of the new row goes into the first real stitch, at the base of that chain.
caption: On 90 stitches a single gained stitch per row is easy to miss. The first hdc goes into the first real stitch.

alt: A folded oatmeal crochet scarf on a wood bench
caption: Illustration. A plain half double crochet rectangle. Not a tested scarf.

alt: Diagram of half double crochet: yarn over before inserting, three loops on the hook, then one pull through all three.
caption: Yarn over once before the hook goes in. Three loops, then one pull through all three.

alt: Diagram comparing 24 half double crochet at 3 per inch, which is 8 inches, with the same 24 stitches at 0.4 inch each, which is 9.6 inches. An 8 inch scarf at that looser gauge needs 20 stitches.
caption: Use the count from the swatch. Twenty-four is only the 3-per-inch case.

alt: A foundation chain of 26. The 2 chains nearest the hook are skipped and the first hdc goes into the 3rd chain from the hook, so row 1 has 24 hdc.
caption: Chain 26 for 24 hdc. The 2 skipped chains next to the hook are the turning chain, not a stitch.

alt: Diagram of a row of stitches with a chain-2 at the end that is skipped. The first half double of the next row goes into the first real stitch.
caption: The chain is turned out of the way. The first half double uses the first stitch of the row you just finished.

alt: A book partly inside an oatmeal crochet sleeve
caption: Illustration. A soft sleeve with the book drawn partway in. Not a fitted sample.

alt: A tape measure on a plain book
caption: Illustration. Width and height of the closed book. The drawing is not the example size.

alt: Oatmeal yarn, a hook, and a plain book
caption: Illustration. The skein is not a weighed yardage for this sleeve.

alt: A wide oatmeal rectangle on the hook
caption: Illustration. The width stays the same on every row.

alt: A needle seaming the side of the sleeve
caption: Illustration. Side seam through both layers. The top stays open.

alt: The sleeve on a sofa with the book inside
caption: Illustration. A soft cover. Not a waterproof wrap.

alt: Diagram of the example arithmetic. A 5 inch cover plus half an inch is 5.5 inches, times 4 stitches is 22. Three quarters of 8 inches is 6, and the fabric before the fold is 12 inches.
caption: The half inch and the three-quarter height are choices. A different book replaces both before you chain.

alt: A foundation chain of 23. The chain nearest the hook is skipped and the first sc goes into the 2nd chain from the hook, so row 1 has 22 sc.
caption: Chain 23 for 22 sc, 5.5 inches at 4 sc per inch.

alt: Two rows of single crochet. Correct: the turning ch 1 sits beside the edge and the first sc of the new row goes into the first stitch, the last one made on the row below, so the count stays the same. Mistake: the first sc goes into the ch 1, outside the edge, which adds a stitch and makes the edge flare.
caption: Sixty rows is a lot of edges. Starting every row in the edge stitch is what keeps the sleeve 22 wide.

alt: Diagram of a 12 inch by 5.5 inch rectangle folded in half to a 6 inch sleeve. The side edges are sewn. The top stays open. The 12 inches and 5.5 inches hold only at the example gauge.
caption: Sixty divided by 5 is 12, and half of 12 is 6. Twenty-two divided by 4 is 5.5. Both divisions use the example gauge.

alt: A cream cotton cozy gathered around a plain bowl
caption: Illustration. Two cotton layers with the corners pinched and a bowl drawn inside. Not a heat test and not a fitted sample.

alt: A tape laid across a plain bowl
caption: Illustration. Measure your bowl. The marks in the drawing are not the example size.

alt: Cream cotton yarn, a hook, and a plain bowl
caption: Illustration. Cotton only. Yardage is not a weighed cozy.

alt: Two cream squares stacked, edges aligned
caption: Illustration. Both squares need the same stitch count before the join.

alt: A corner pinched and sewn so the side stands up
caption: Illustration. The pinch length comes from your bowl. Two inches is the example that fails the 3 inch wall.

alt: The cozy on a table with a plain bowl set inside
caption: Illustration. A table holder in the drawing. Heat behavior was not tested.

alt: Diagram of a square whose side is the rim diameter plus the wall height on the left and again on the right. The corners are marked as extra fabric to pinch. The example is 6 plus 3 plus 3 equals 12 inches.
caption: Planning sketch. The dashed middle is the rim diameter, not the base. The corners are surplus.

alt: A foundation chain of 49. The chain nearest the hook is skipped and the first sc goes into the 2nd chain from the hook, so row 1 has 48 sc.
caption: Chain 49 for 48 sc, 12 inches at 4 sc per inch. Make two squares from the same count.

alt: Two rows of single crochet. Correct: the turning ch 1 sits beside the edge and the first sc of the new row goes into the first stitch, the last one made on the row below, so the count stays the same. Mistake: the first sc goes into the ch 1, outside the edge, which adds a stitch and makes the edge flare.
caption: Two squares only match if both keep 48. The first stitch of each row goes in the edge stitch.

alt: Diagram comparing 48 single crochets along the top of a 12 inch square with 60 single crochets if every row end is used. Four single crochets for every five row ends brings the side back to 48.
caption: Worked for the example gauge only. The equal count is arithmetic, not a promise that the join lies flat. Recount the groups if your swatch is not 4 stitches and 5 rows to the inch.

alt: Diagram of a square with a pinch at each corner. The flat center is about the side minus two pinches. The example is 12 minus 2 minus 2 equals 8 inches.
caption: The 8 inches is arithmetic from a 2 inch pinch. It is the check against the base, not a length to sew without the bowl.

alt: An oatmeal crochet strap around a coiled white cable
caption: Illustration. A buttoned strap around one coil. Not a strap measured on a cable.

alt: Oatmeal yarn, a hook, and a wood button
caption: Illustration. Yarn, hook, and button. Not a weighed amount.

alt: A coiled cable with a paper strip around the bundle, 4 inches in the example. Below, the strap laid flat with a button 3 rows from the start and a buttonhole on the last row. The distance between them is 4 inches. The total is 0.6 plus 4 plus 0.2, which is 4.8 inches, or 24 rows at 5 rows per inch.
caption: The strap's working length is the button-to-buttonhole distance. The rest is margin.

alt: A foundation chain of 9. The chain nearest the hook is skipped and the first sc goes into the 2nd chain from the hook, so row 1 has 8 sc.
caption: Step 1. Chain 9 for an 8-stitch strap, about 2 inches wide at 4 sc per inch.

alt: Two rows of single crochet. Correct: the turning ch 1 sits beside the edge and the first sc of the new row goes into the first stitch, the last one made on the row below, so the count stays the same. Mistake: the first sc goes into the ch 1, outside the edge, which adds a stitch and makes the edge flare.
caption: A narrow strap shows a gained stitch at once. Start each row in the edge stitch, not the ch 1.

alt: Buttonhole row over 8 stitches: sc 3, ch 3 over 2 skipped stitches, sc 3. Rows 1 to 23 are 8 sc. The button goes on row 3, centered.
caption: Step 2. The ch 3 spans 2 skipped stitches. One extra chain keeps the hole from pinching the button.

alt: A green crochet pocket with a blank card and a pine sprig
caption: Illustration. A green pocket with a red edge and a blank card. Not a pocket fitted to a card.

alt: Green and red yarn, a hook, and a blank card
caption: Illustration. The card is a size check. Not a weighed amount of yarn.

alt: The flat rectangle, 16 stitches by 24 rows, with a fold after row 9. Folded, the front is 9 rows or 1.8 inches, the back is 15 rows or 3.0 inches, and a 2.125 inch card shows about a third of an inch above the red front edge. A note says folding in the middle gives 2.4 inches per side and the card sinks 0.27 inch below the opening.
caption: The front is shorter than the card on purpose. The visible strip is how the card comes out.

alt: A foundation chain of 17. The chain nearest the hook is skipped and the first sc goes into the 2nd chain from the hook, so row 1 has 16 sc.
caption: Step 1. Chain 17 for 16 sc, about 4 inches wide.

alt: Drawn to scale. A flat piece 16 sc, 4 in wide and 24 rows, 4.8 in tall, folded at the dashed line into a pocket. Right sides out. Seam both sides through both layers for the 9 front rows. Front: rows 1 to 9, 1.8 in. Back: rows 10 to 24, 3.0 in. A 2.125 in card shows about 0.33 in above the front.
caption: Step 2. Drawn to scale. The fold is off center: 9 rows in front, 15 behind, so the card shows above the front.

alt: A finished green crochet Christmas tree standing on a wooden table
caption: Illustration. The intended look. Not a measured sample.

alt: Hands crocheting a green cone in the round for a Christmas tree
caption: Illustration. Work in a spiral and mark the first stitch of every round.

alt: A green crochet Christmas tree being stuffed
caption: Illustration. Stuff firmly and weight the base.

alt: Sewing a brown trunk onto a crochet Christmas tree
caption: Illustration. Add decorations after the shape is stable.

alt: Three cones worked from the tip down. About 1.5 stitches added per round makes a slim cone, about 2 makes the tree on this page, about 3 makes a squat cone, and 6 lies flat. Below, two flat triangles: decreasing both ends every row makes a low triangle, and every other row makes a taller tree shape.
caption: Average stitches added per round decide the cone. Rows between decreases decide the triangle.

alt: Four steps. 1: wrap the yarn around two fingers so the tail crosses over the working yarn. 2: insert the hook under the ring, catch the working yarn, and pull up a loop, then ch 1; the ch 1 is not a stitch. 3: work the stated number of sc into the ring, over both strands of the ring and the tail. 4: pull the tail to close the center, then count the stitches.
caption: Round 1 starts in a magic ring, pulled tight so the top has no hole.

alt: Tiered cone tree, round by round, as bars sized by stitch count. Rounds 1 to 2: 6, Round 3: 9, Round 4: 9, Round 5: 12, Round 6: 12, Round 7: 18, Round 8: 18, Round 9: 18, Round 10: 24, Round 11: 24, Round 12: 24, Round 13: 30, Round 14: 30, Round 15: 30, Round 16: 36, Rounds 17 to 18: 36, Round 19: 36, Round 20: 30, Round 21: 24, Round 22: 18, Round 23: 12, Round 24: 6. Rounds 9, 12 and 15 are back loops only, one per tier. Round 19 is the back-loop fold for the base, then rounds 20 to 24 close it.
caption: The cone by stitch count. Each terracotta round is worked in back loops, leaving the ledge that makes a tier.

alt: An oatmeal chunky crochet beanie with a folded brim
caption: Illustration. A bulky hat with the brim folded once. Not a fitted sample.

alt: A skein of bulky oatmeal yarn and a large hook
caption: Illustration. Start with the hook on the label, then swatch.

alt: A ribbed oatmeal crochet band
caption: Illustration. Back-loop single crochet makes the rib. The band is flat.

alt: The hat body worked upward from the brim
caption: Illustration. The body is worked in the round from the band.

alt: The crown of the hat decreasing inward
caption: Illustration. Decreases pull the top closed.

alt: A sideways ribbed brim is counted in rows and the body in stitches. The example brim is 60 rows for 20 inches at 3 rows per inch. The body needs 50 stitches at 2.5 stitches per inch, so work 5 single crochet over every 6 row ends, skipping one. One stitch per row would make 60 stitches, a 24 inch body that flares.
caption: Work out the body count from the body gauge, then spread it along the brim's row ends.

alt: A foundation chain of 9. The chain nearest the hook is skipped and the first sc goes into the 2nd chain from the hook, so row 1 has 8 sc.
caption: Step 1. Chain 9 for an 8-stitch brim. The chain is the brim's height, not the hat's width.

alt: Two steps. 1: the top of each stitch has a front loop, nearer you, and a back loop, farther away. For the rib, insert the hook under the back loop only. 2: the front loops left behind form a raised ridge on every row. The fabric stretches across the ridges, in the direction the rows stack up, so a band worked sideways stretches around the head.
caption: Back loop only on every row from row 2 makes the stretchy rib.

alt: Crown round 1: 50 to 45, drawn as rings from the center out. Body: undefined, 50 stitches. Crown 1: (sc 8, sc2tog) 5 times, 45 stitches.
caption: Step 3. Five decreases a round, spaced evenly, keep the crown flat.

alt: The crown by stitch count, as bars sized by stitch count. Round 0: 50, Round 1: 45, Round 2: 40, Round 3: 35, Round 4: 30, Round 5: 25, Round 6: 20, Round 7: 15, Round 8: 10, Round 9: 5. R0 is the last even body round. Each crown round removes 5.
caption: Step 4. The crown by stitch count: 50 down to 5 in nine rounds, then the gap is closed with the tail.

alt: A small rust-orange crochet leaf on linen
caption: Illustration. The flat leaf this page describes. Not a photograph of a made sample.

alt: A chain of 9 with the first chain from the hook skipped. Above the chain, stitches rise and fall: single crochet, half double, four double crochet, half double, single crochet. At the far end, 3 single crochet in one chain make the tip. Below, the return side mirrors the heights in 7 chains: half double, four double, half double, single crochet. 17 stitches make a pointed oval.
caption: Heights rise and fall along each side of the chain. Three stitches in the end chain turn the corner and make the tip.

alt: A white crochet ghost drawstring bag with black eyes
caption: Illustration. A white bag with eyes and a drawstring top. Not a measured sample.

alt: White yarn, black yarn, a hook, and a needle
caption: Illustration. Yarn and a hook. Not a weighed amount.

alt: A drawstring threaded through the top of a white bag
caption: Illustration. The cord runs through the eyelet round.

alt: Two eyelet rounds compared on 54 stitches. Single crochet, chain 1, skip 1 makes 27 small holes for a thin chain cord and many small gathers. Single crochet 4, chain 2, skip 2, nine times, makes 9 larger holes 1.5 inches apart for a thicker cord and fewer, deeper folds. The next round puts 2 single crochet in each chain-2 space to return to 54.
caption: Small, close holes close tighter. Large, spaced holes take a thicker cord. Both need a stitch count the repeat divides into.

alt: Base: rounds 1 to 9, drawn as rings from the center out. Round 1: 6 sc in a magic ring, 6 stitches. Round 2: 2 sc in each st, 12 stitches. Round 3: (sc, 2 sc in next) 6 times, 18 stitches. Round 4: (sc 2, 2 sc in next) 6 times, 24 stitches. Round 5: (sc 3, 2 sc in next) 6 times, 30 stitches. Round 6: (sc 4, 2 sc in next) 6 times, 36 stitches. Round 7: (sc 5, 2 sc in next) 6 times, 42 stitches. Round 8: (sc 6, 2 sc in next) 6 times, 48 stitches. Round 9: (sc 7, 2 sc in next) 6 times, 54 stitches.
caption: Step 1. Nine rounds of 6 increases give a 54-stitch base, about 4.3 inches across.

alt: Round 33: nine large eyelets, drawn as rings from the center out. Round 32: undefined, 54 stitches. Round 33: (sc 4, ch 2, skip 2) 9 times: 36 sc, 36 stitches. Each open circle is one ch-2 space over 2 skipped stitches.
caption: Step 2. Nine ch-2 spaces, 6 stitches apart. Round 34 puts 2 sc in each space to restore 54.

alt: A small white crochet ghost coin pouch with a drawstring and coins beside it
caption: Illustration. A white pouch with a face and a drawstring. Not a measured sample.

alt: White yarn, a hook, a needle, scissors, and a few quarters
caption: Illustration. Materials. Not a weighed amount of yarn.

alt: A yarn drawstring woven through the top of a white pouch
caption: Illustration. The cord goes through the eyelet round, not through the solid rounds above it.

alt: The eyelet round opened into a line of single crochet blocks with chain arches between them, 15 repeats over 30 stitches. A cord weaves out through one hole and in through the next. A second strip shows 31 stitches, where the last repeat ends on a solid stitch next to the first and the hole is missing. Cord length: 7.5 inches around plus two 4 inch tails, 15.5 inches.
caption: Every repeat uses two stitches. An odd count leaves one over, and that stitch closes a hole.

alt: Four steps. 1: wrap the yarn around two fingers so the tail crosses over the working yarn. 2: insert the hook under the ring, catch the working yarn, and pull up a loop, then ch 1; the ch 1 is not a stitch. 3: work the stated number of sc into the ring, over both strands of the ring and the tail. 4: pull the tail to close the center, then count the stitches.
caption: Round 1 starts in a magic ring. Pull the tail tight before Round 2.

alt: Base: rounds 1 to 5, drawn as rings from the center out. Round 1: 6 sc in a magic ring, 6 stitches. Round 2: 2 sc in each st, 12 stitches. Round 3: (sc, 2 sc in next) 6 times, 18 stitches. Round 4: (sc 2, 2 sc in next) 6 times, 24 stitches. Round 5: (sc 3, 2 sc in next) 6 times, 30 stitches.
caption: Step 1. Six increases a round. Round 5 ends on 30, an even count, which the eyelet round needs.

alt: The whole pouch by stitch count, as bars sized by stitch count. Round 1: 6, Round 2: 12, Round 3: 18, Round 4: 24, Rounds 5 to 15: 30, Round 16: 15+15, Round 17: 30, Round 18: 30. Round 16 is the eyelet round: (sc, ch 1, skip 1) 15 times. Round 17 puts 1 sc in each sc and each space, back to 30.
caption: Step 2. The whole pouch by stitch count. The eyelet round, 16, keeps 30 stitches: 15 sc and 15 chains.

alt: A finished crochet Christmas gnome with tall hat and beard
caption: Illustration. The intended look. Not a measured sample.

alt: Hands crocheting a round gnome body in the round
caption: Illustration. The body is worked in the round.

alt: Sewing a pointed hat onto a crochet gnome
caption: Illustration. The hat goes on last so it covers the joins.

alt: Side view of a gnome. The body widens from 30 stitches at the top to 36 and 42, then a back-loop round and decreases make a flat base with a weight bag inside. The hat runs from a floppy tip down to 42 stitches, slightly wider than the 36-stitch body it covers, with its brim touching the top of the nose. The beard hangs below the nose.
caption: The body widens toward the base. The hat covers the top half, and its brim sits on the nose.

alt: Four steps. 1: wrap the yarn around two fingers so the tail crosses over the working yarn. 2: insert the hook under the ring, catch the working yarn, and pull up a loop, then ch 1; the ch 1 is not a stitch. 3: work the stated number of sc into the ring, over both strands of the ring and the tail. 4: pull the tail to close the center, then count the stitches.
caption: Round 1 starts in a magic ring, pulled tight so the top has no hole.

alt: Gnome body, top down, as bars sized by stitch count. Round 1: 6, Round 2: 12, Round 3: 18, Round 4: 24, Round 5: 30, Rounds 6 to 7: 30, Round 8: 36, Rounds 9 to 10: 36, Round 11: 42, Rounds 12 to 14: 42, Round 15: 42, Round 16: 36, Round 17: 30, Round 18: 24, Round 19: 18, Round 20: 12, Round 21: 6. Round 15 (terracotta) is back loops only at 42. Rounds 16 to 21 remove 6 each to close a flat base.
caption: The body widens in steps with even rounds between, then the back-loop round 15 turns the base flat.

alt: Gnome hat, tip down, as bars sized by stitch count. Rounds 1 to 4: 6, Round 5: 9, Rounds 6 to 7: 9, Round 8: 12, Rounds 9 to 10: 12, Round 11: 18, Round 12: 18, Round 13: 24, Round 14: 24, Round 15: 30, Round 16: 30, Round 17: 36, Round 18: 36, Round 19: 42, Rounds 20 to 21: 42. A thin tip first: 3 added every third round to 12. Then 6 every other round to 42.
caption: The hat ends at 42, the same as the body, so it sits over the top instead of perching on it.

alt: A cream cotton tote made of granny squares with two straps
caption: Illustration. It draws a different square motif and a boxed base. This page makes two flat panels with no base. Not a finished sample.

alt: Worsted cotton, a hook, and a yarn needle
caption: Illustration. Worsted cotton and tools. Not a weighed amount.

alt: A finished granny square beside a hook
caption: Illustration. A granny square with an extra border. It is not this page's 4-round square. Measure the square you make.

alt: A front panel and a back panel, each four squares in a 2 by 2 grid. Each panel edge is 19 plus 19, which is 38 single crochet. The two panels joined along the sides and bottom with a dashed seam, top open, with two straps. A bar shows one panel's 34-stitch top edge split 8, strap 5, 8, strap 5, 8.
caption: Two flat panels and three seams. Every number on the drawing follows from the 4-round square.

alt: Granny square round 1. Four clusters of three double crochet worked into the ring, 12 double crochet in all, with a chain-2 corner between each pair. There are no side spaces yet.
caption: Round 1: four clusters with a ch-2 corner between each. The ch 3 counts as the first dc.

alt: Granny square round 2. 24 double crochet in all. Each of the four corners holds 3 dc, ch 2, 3 dc. Each side has 1 chain-1 space, still empty; round 3 fills them.
caption: Round 2: each corner space gets two clusters, and a ch 1 sits between corners.

alt: Granny square round 4. 48 double crochet in all. Each of the four corners holds 3 dc, ch 2, 3 dc. Each side has 3 chain-1 spaces and 2 clusters worked into the chain-1 spaces of the round below.
caption: Round 4: the corner spaces (ch 2) and the side spaces (ch 1) are worked differently. Mixing them up is the usual reason a square twists.

alt: One side of a granny square, round 3 worked over round 2. Correct: the side cluster of round 3 sits in the chain-1 space between round 2's two corner halves, with a chain-1 on each side of it. Common mistake: the cluster goes into the top of a double crochet instead. The gap closes, the side goes stiff, and the square starts to cup.
caption: Clusters go in the gaps between the clusters below, never on top of them.

alt: One edge of a 4-round square from corner to corner: a corner chain-2 space, four 3 double crochet clusters with three chain-1 spaces between them, and the next corner space. Two single crochet in each corner space, one in each of the 12 double crochet, and one in each chain-1 space, for 2 plus 12 plus 3 plus 2, 19. The formula 4n plus 3 gives 19 for 4 rounds, 23 for 5, and 27 for 6.
caption: Both squares in a seam have the same edge, so both layers take the same 19 stitches. That is what keeps the seam flat.

alt: Two steps. 1: hold the pieces wrong sides together with the edges lined up stitch for stitch. 2: insert the hook through both layers at once, matching stitch to stitch, and work one sc in each pair; work 3 sc in a corner stitch to turn a corner flat.
caption: Squares are joined right sides together with one sc in each stitch and space along the edge, 19 per square.

alt: An oatmeal crochet hooded scarf with the hood open
caption: Illustration. Intended look of a long scarf with a hood at the center. Not a worn sample, and not the 12 inch panel.

alt: A long oatmeal crochet rectangle
caption: Illustration. The scarf is one rectangle. The hood is a separate rectangle.

alt: Two skeins of oatmeal yarn and a hook
caption: Illustration. The skeins are not a weighed yardage for this scarf.

alt: The hood rectangle folded and partly seamed
caption: Illustration of the fold and a back seam. The face edge stays open. This drawing is not the 12 inch panel on a person.

alt: The hood sewn to the center of the scarf
caption: Illustration. Center the hood on one edge. A hood near one end is a scarf with a lump.

alt: The scarf draped on a chair
caption: Illustration. Ends hang. A chair is not a head and not a size.

alt: Diagram of a rectangle of width W and height H, folded in half so the fold is center back. The crown is seamed. The open edge remains the full width W, and the depth is half of W.
caption: The opening is the width you chained, not half of it, and not the row count. Adding rows makes the hood taller. It does not enlarge the opening.

alt: Diagram of half double crochet: yarn over before inserting, three loops on the hook, then one pull through all three.
caption: The stitch itself is not the sizing problem. The width of the rectangle is.

alt: Diagram of a straight crochet edge beside a slanted edge. The slant is a row that gained or lost a stitch, often at the turning chain.
caption: Same stitch count every row keeps the side straight. A gained stitch at the turning chain is the usual slant.

alt: A foundation chain of 26. The 2 chains nearest the hook are skipped and the first hdc goes into the 3rd chain from the hook, so row 1 has 24 hdc.
caption: Chain 26 for 24 hdc. On this page the 2 skipped chains do not count, so the row is 24, not 26.

alt: Diagram of a long scarf with the hood sewn along the center of one long edge. The seam does not cross the width of the scarf.
caption: Center is along the length. The seam stays on the near edge.

alt: A cream crochet lace bandana worn tied at the nape
caption: Illustration. A worn cotton bandana with ties at the nape. The drawn mesh is not a stitch map of this pattern, and no sample was made.

alt: Cream yarn and a hook
caption: Illustration. DK cotton and a hook. Not a weighed amount.

alt: Close view of cream granny clusters
caption: Illustration of the cluster texture. Not a stitch map. In this pattern every inner shell sits in a chain space.

alt: Diagram of nested V-shaped rows. The first row sits at the middle of a straight top edge. Each larger V has its ends on that edge and its corner further down, and the corners stack into the point. A note says that with a square point the depth is half the long edge, so 16 inches gives 8.
caption: The start is the middle of the long edge. The point is the last corner you work, not the first.

alt: A chain of 4. Every stitch of row 1 goes into the 4th chain from the hook: 2 double crochet, a chain-2 corner, then 3 double crochet. The 3 skipped chains stand up as the first double crochet, so the row has 6 double crochet and one corner.
caption: Step 1. All of row 1 goes into one chain. The 3 skipped chains count as the first dc on this page.

alt: Row 2 drawn as four 3 double crochet shells with chain-1 dots after the first and before the last, and a chain-2 corner in the middle, for 12 double crochet and two chain-1 spaces. A table gives row 1 as 6 double crochet, row 2 as 12, row 3 as 18, row 4 as 24, and row n as 6n with 2 times n minus 1 chain-1 spaces.
caption: Each row adds 6 double crochet: one shell at each end of the long edge. The corner only moves.

alt: The bandana drawn as nested V shapes hanging from the long edge. Each row is a V with its corner at the point. Row 4 is drawn in full: four shells of three double crochet on each arm, counting the corner halves, one ch-2 corner at the point, and six ch-1 spaces. Row n has 6n double crochet: 6, 12, 18, 24.
caption: Step 2. Every row adds one shell to each arm and keeps one corner, so the counts go 6, 12, 18, 24.

alt: A gray crochet sleeve with a closed laptop partway in
caption: Illustration. A soft sleeve around a closed laptop. Not water protection and not a drop test.

alt: Gray worsted cotton, a hook, and a closed laptop
caption: Illustration. Yarn and a hook. Not a weighed amount.

alt: A needle seaming the side, with a second pass at the bottom corner
caption: Illustration. Side seams only. The top stays open. The corner is reinforced.

alt: A long rectangle 53 stitches wide and 90 rows long, folded after row 45. For a 12 by 8.5 by 0.6 inch laptop: width 12 plus 0.6 plus 0.25 plus 0.25 is 13.1 inches, 53 stitches; depth per side 8.5 plus 0.3 plus 0.2 is 9 inches, 90 rows. A note says to measure flat, because a long cotton piece grows when it hangs.
caption: The thickness is added to the width. On a thin laptop that is half an inch; on a thick one, an inch or more.

alt: A foundation chain of 54. The chain nearest the hook is skipped and the first sc goes into the 2nd chain from the hook, so row 1 has 53 sc.
caption: Step 1. Chain 54 for 53 sc. A larger hook for the chain keeps the bottom edge from pulling in.

alt: Rows 2 to 90: 53 sc. Rows of 53 sc drawn one symbol per stitch and worked back and forth, each starting with a turning chain (ch 1, not a st). Row 46 is highlighted. Every row: 53 sc. Count every 10 rows. The fold falls between rows 45 and 46.
caption: Step 2. 53 sc on every row. Counting every 10 rows catches a gained stitch before it costs width.

alt: Drawn to scale. A flat piece 53 sc, 13.1 in wide and 90 rows, 18 in tall, folded at the dashed line into a pocket. Right sides together. Sc through both layers, one per row end. Reinforce the bottom corners.
caption: Step 3. Drawn to scale: 13.1 by 18 inches folds into a 13.1 by 9 inch sleeve.

alt: Two steps. 1: hold the pieces wrong sides together with the edges lined up stitch for stitch. 2: insert the hook through both layers at once, matching stitch to stitch, and work one sc in each pair; work 3 sc in a corner stitch to turn a corner flat.
caption: One sc per row end through both layers, from the fold to the top.

alt: A dusty rose crochet lip balm holder on a key ring
caption: Illustration. It draws the loop on the closed end with the tube pointing down. This page sews the loop at the rim instead.

alt: Rose yarn, a hook, a key ring, and an unmarked lip balm tube
caption: Illustration. Materials. The tube is the size guide.

alt: The holder clipped to a bag
caption: Illustration. Hung from the rim, base down, cap up. The arrangement this page uses.

alt: Two sleeves hanging from rings. Left: loop on the closed base, sleeve upside down, tube sliding out of the rim. Right: loop at the rim, base hanging down, cap up. Note: 9 stitches at 4 per inch is 2.25 inches around, and a 0.65 inch tube is 2.04 inches around.
caption: The loop end is the top. Put it at the rim and the closed base becomes the bottom.

alt: Four steps. 1: wrap the yarn around two fingers so the tail crosses over the working yarn. 2: insert the hook under the ring, catch the working yarn, and pull up a loop, then ch 1; the ch 1 is not a stitch. 3: work the stated number of sc into the ring, over both strands of the ring and the tail. 4: pull the tail to close the center, then count the stitches.
caption: The magic ring closes completely, so the base has no hole for the tube to push through.

alt: Base: rounds 1 and 2, drawn as rings from the center out. Round 1: 6 sc in a magic ring, 6 stitches. Round 2: (sc, 2 sc in next) 3 times, 9 stitches.
caption: Step 1. Only 3 increases: the base cups on purpose and starts the tube.

alt: The whole holder by stitch count, as bars sized by stitch count. Round 1: 6, Round 2: 9, Rounds 3 to 12: 9. Rounds 3 to 12 are even, so the fabric turns straight up into a tube.
caption: Step 2. Nine stitches on every round from Round 2 to Round 12. The tube is about 2.25 inches around at 4 sc per inch.

alt: A small cotton drawstring pouch
caption: Illustration. A closed rectangle with a tie at the top. Not a tested pouch.

alt: Worsted cotton, a hook, and a short crochet chain for a tie
caption: Illustration. Cotton. The tie is a chain. Not a weighed amount.

alt: A chain woven through eyelets at the top of the pouch
caption: Illustration. The tie starts and ends at the front.

alt: A folded pouch, 28 stitches wide and 25 rows tall per side, with items inside and a drawstring near the top. Width: 5.75 widest plus 0.75 thickest plus 0.5 ease is 7 inches, 28 stitches. Height: 3.5 tallest plus 1.5 for the gather is 5 inches per side, 50 rows in all.
caption: Thickness counts as width. Gathering needs height. Both come from the contents.

alt: A foundation chain of 29. The chain nearest the hook is skipped and the first sc goes into the 2nd chain from the hook, so row 1 has 28 sc.
caption: Step 1. Chain 29 for 28 sc. The foundation edge becomes half of the opening, so keep it loose.

alt: Two rows of single crochet. Correct: the turning ch 1 sits beside the edge and the first sc of the new row goes into the first stitch, the last one made on the row below, so the count stays the same. Mistake: the first sc goes into the ch 1, outside the edge, which adds a stitch and makes the edge flare.
caption: The first sc of each row goes into the edge stitch, not the ch 1. That keeps 28 stitches, and the opening count of 56.

alt: Drawn to scale. A flat piece 28 sc, 7 in wide and 50 rows, 10 in tall, folded at the dashed line into a pocket. Right sides together. Sc through both layers up each side, one sc per row end.
caption: Step 2. Drawn to scale: a 7 by 10 inch rectangle folds into a 7 by 5 inch pouch. Row 1 and row 50 together make the 56-stitch opening.

alt: Two steps. 1: hold the pieces wrong sides together with the edges lined up stitch for stitch. 2: insert the hook through both layers at once, matching stitch to stitch, and work one sc in each pair; work 3 sc in a corner stitch to turn a corner flat.
caption: Each side seam is one sc in each row end, through both layers, starting in the fold itself.

alt: A natural cotton market bag with mesh sides and two handles
caption: Illustration. Solid base, open mesh, two handles. Not a load test.

alt: Natural cotton yarn, a hook, and a yarn needle
caption: Illustration. Yarn, hook, and needle. Not a weighed amount.

alt: A flat cotton circle in single crochet
caption: Illustration. The base is solid single crochet. Measure it before the mesh starts.

alt: Handle ends sewn across the solid top band
caption: Illustration. Each handle end spans many stitches. There is no weight number on this bag.

alt: The bag in profile: a flat base of 96 single crochet, about 7.6 inches across, one even round, mesh rounds of 48 double crochet and 48 chain-1 spaces, and a top band of 96 single crochet. Beside it, half the band, 48 stitches, split 10, handle end 8, 12, handle end 8, 10, repeated on the other half.
caption: Solid where it needs strength, open where it needs to be light. The handles go only into the solid band.

alt: Four steps. 1: wrap the yarn around two fingers so the tail crosses over the working yarn. 2: insert the hook under the ring, catch the working yarn, and pull up a loop, then ch 1; the ch 1 is not a stitch. 3: work the stated number of sc into the ring, over both strands of the ring and the tail. 4: pull the tail to close the center, then count the stitches.
caption: The base starts in a magic ring.

alt: Base: rounds 1 to 17, as bars sized by stitch count. Round 1: 6, Round 2: 12, Round 3: 18, Round 4: 24, Round 5: 30, Round 6: 36, Round 7: 42, Round 8: 48, Round 9: 54, Round 10: 60, Round 11: 66, Round 12: 72, Round 13: 78, Round 14: 84, Round 15: 90, Round 16: 96, Round 17: 96. Round 16 is 96, about 7.6 in across. Round 17 is even and starts the turn.
caption: Step 1. Sixteen rounds of six increases each. Round 16 is 96.

alt: Correct: the increase in each round is moved, for example by working half the plain stitches before the first increase on alternate rounds, so the edge stays round. Mistake: every increase lands directly above the last one, which builds six corners and the circle becomes a hexagon.
caption: Sixteen rounds of stacked increases make a clear hexagon. Moving them keeps the base round.

alt: Mesh round 1 on 96, drawn as rings from the center out. Round 17: undefined, 96 stitches. Mesh round 1: (dc in next, ch 1, skip 1) around: 48 dc, 48 stitches. Count the dc every few rounds. 47 or 49 means a unit was lost or added.
caption: Step 3. The mesh: 48 dc with a chain space over every skipped stitch. The ch 3 counts as the first dc.

alt: A small oatmeal crochet bag with a short strap
caption: Illustration. A small rectangle bag and a short strap. Not a fitted sample.

alt: Oatmeal worsted cotton, a hook, and a yarn needle
caption: Illustration. Yarn and a hook. Not a weighed amount.

alt: A short strap sewn inside the top of the bag
caption: Illustration. Each strap end is sewn through many stitches at the side seam.

alt: A foundation chain of 28. The chain nearest the hook is skipped and the first sc goes into the 2nd chain from the hook, so row 1 has 27 sc.
caption: Step 1. Chain 28 for 27 sc, 6.75 inches at 4 sc per inch.

alt: Two rows of single crochet. Correct: the turning ch 1 sits beside the edge and the first sc of the new row goes into the first stitch, the last one made on the row below, so the count stays the same. Mistake: the first sc goes into the ch 1, outside the edge, which adds a stitch and makes the edge flare.
caption: Each row starts in the edge stitch. A gained stitch here shows up as a crooked side seam.

alt: Drawn to scale. A flat piece 27 sc, 6.75 in wide and 65 rows, 13 in tall, folded at the dashed line into a pocket. Seam both sides, then work 27 sc along row 65 and 27 along the foundation chain.
caption: Step 2. Drawn to scale. The 65 rows fold in half to about 6.5 inches a side, and the top round joins both edges: 54 sc.

alt: A foundation chain of 5. The chain nearest the hook is skipped and the first sc goes into the 2nd chain from the hook, so row 1 has 4 sc.
caption: Step 3. The strap is a narrow strip: chain 5 for 4 sc.

alt: The strap end overlapping the inside of the bag by about an inch at the side seam, sewn with a box and an X through strap and wall. A single corner stitch is marked as the version that tears out. A test list: fill the bag, pin the second end, hang it for a day, remeasure, then sew.
caption: The strap's length is decided after it has carried weight, not before.

alt: Five illustrated crochet phone sleeves in different colors
caption: Illustration. Five colorways of the same rectangle. Not a sleeve measured on a phone.

alt: An iPhone 18 Pro Max beside a tape measure, yarn, and a hook
caption: Illustration. Measure against the phone you own, not a smaller one.

alt: Joining terracotta yarn on the last loop of a cream stitch
caption: Illustration. Change color on the last yarn-over so the new row starts clean.

alt: Looking down into a sleeve with a phone inside. The fabric runs around the phone's 3.07 inch face and its 0.34 inch edges, with a seam at each side. Notes: fabric all the way round is 2 times 3.41, which is 6.82 inches, so each flat face is 3.41 inches before seams, about 3.9 inches with seams and ease, 16 single crochet at 4 per inch rather than 13.
caption: The sleeve has to cover the phone's edges as well as its face. That is the 0.34 inch most first sleeves forget.

alt: A foundation chain of 17. The chain nearest the hook is skipped and the first sc goes into the 2nd chain from the hook, so row 1 has 16 sc. Checkpoint: the first row lying flat measures about 3.9 in.
caption: Step 1. The chain next to the hook is skipped and does not count, so 17 chains give 16 sc.

alt: Two rows of single crochet. Correct: the turning ch 1 sits beside the edge and the first sc of the new row goes into the first stitch, the last one made on the row below, so the count stays the same. Mistake: the first sc goes into the ch 1, outside the edge, which adds a stitch and makes the edge flare.
caption: Where the first stitch of each row goes. Working into the ch 1 is the usual reason a 16-stitch sleeve grows to 17.

alt: Rows 2 to 70: 16 sc every row. Rows of 16 sc drawn one symbol per stitch and worked back and forth, each starting with a turning chain (ch 1, not a st). Row 36 is highlighted. Every row: 16 sc. Count every 10 rows. Row 35 is the middle. With 70 rows, the fold lands between rows 35 and 36.
caption: Step 2. The same 16 stitches on every row. The two halves of the sleeve meet at the middle row.

alt: Drawn to scale. A flat piece 16 sc, 3.9 in wide and 70 rows, 14 in tall, folded at the dashed line into a pocket. Right side in. Whipstitch each side from the fold up, through the outer loops only. Top stays open. Each side ends up about 7 in deep: the phone's 6.43 in plus the fold and a collar.
caption: Step 3. Drawn to scale: a 3.9 by 14 inch strip folds into a 3.9 by 7 inch pocket.

alt: Two edges laid side by side, right sides together. Correct: the needle passes through the outer loop of each edge stitch only, so the seam is flat and takes almost no width. Mistake: the needle goes through the whole stitch on both sides, which builds a thick ridge and takes width from the inside.
caption: A seam through the outer loops keeps the inside width the sleeve was sized for.

alt: A cotton phone sleeve on a long crossbody strap
caption: Illustration. A small sleeve and one long strap. Not a tested fit.

alt: Cotton yarn, a hook, and a plain phone
caption: Illustration. Cotton. Fuzzy yarn traps grit against the phone. Not a weighed amount.

alt: A long strap sewn to the side of a small sleeve
caption: Illustration. One strap, sewn at both top corners. Not a chain.

alt: A torso outline with a string running from the bag at one hip, across the chest, over the opposite shoulder, down the back, and back to the hip. The loop is 52 inches in the example. The strap is 52 minus the bag's 3.75 inch top edge, about 48 inches, 240 rows. Measuring shoulder to hip on the front only gives about half.
caption: The sleeve's own top edge completes the loop, so subtract its width from the string.

alt: A foundation chain of 16. The chain nearest the hook is skipped and the first sc goes into the 2nd chain from the hook, so row 1 has 15 sc.
caption: Step 1. Chain 16 for 15 sc, 3.75 inches: the phone's width plus its thickness, seams, and ease.

alt: Drawn to scale. A flat piece 15 sc, 3.75 in wide and 67 rows, 13.4 in tall, folded at the dashed line into a pocket. Fold so row 1 meets row 67. Seam both sides. The top stays open.
caption: Step 2. To scale: 67 rows, about 13.4 inches, fold to a sleeve about 6.7 inches deep.

alt: A flap of 7 rows worked over 7 of the 15 stitches on the last round, with a chain loop on the top row. Rows 1 to 6: 7 sc. Row 7: sc 2, ch 4, skip 3, sc 2.
caption: Step 3. The flap covers the middle 7 of the 15 back stitches. On row 7 the ch 4 spans 3 skipped stitches.

alt: A finished orange crochet pumpkin with vertical grooves and a short brown stem
caption: Illustration. The intended shape. Not a measured sample.

alt: Hands crocheting an orange sphere in the round, the sides curving upward
caption: Illustration. Increase until the circle is wide enough, then the sides turn up.

alt: An orange crochet sphere being stuffed and closed with a yarn needle through the last stitches
caption: Illustration. Stuff firmly while the opening is still wide.

alt: A length of yarn wrapped around a stuffed orange ball and pulled tight to form a groove
caption: Illustration. The grooves are cinched from the outside, not crocheted in.

alt: A small crocheted brown tube and a green leaf shape lying beside a tapestry needle
caption: Illustration. Stem and optional leaf, made separately and sewn on.

alt: Side view of a stuffed shape in three bands. Rounds 1 to 6 increase 6 stitches a round to 36. Even rounds at 36 set the height. Decrease rounds go back to 6. About 6 even rounds makes a near ball, about 4 makes a squat pumpkin. A top view shows 6 yarn wraps making 6 grooves.
caption: Increase for width, work even for height, decrease to close. The grooves come later, from the outside.

alt: Four steps. 1: wrap the yarn around two fingers so the tail crosses over the working yarn. 2: insert the hook under the ring, catch the working yarn, and pull up a loop, then ch 1; the ch 1 is not a stitch. 3: work the stated number of sc into the ring, over both strands of the ring and the tail. 4: pull the tail to close the center, then count the stitches.
caption: Round 1 starts in a magic ring, pulled tight so the top has no hole.

alt: Three steps. 1: insert the hook into the front loop only of the next stitch. 2: without pulling through, insert into the front loop of the stitch after it, so three loops are on the hook. 3: yarn over and pull through the two front loops, then yarn over and pull through the two loops on the hook. Two stitches become one.
caption: Through the front loops only, the decrease disappears into the fabric.

alt: An orange crochet pumpkin bag with a green stem and wrapped candy
caption: Illustration. An orange bag, green stem, drawstring. Not a measured sample.

alt: Orange yarn, green yarn, a hook, and a needle
caption: Illustration. Yarn and tools. Not a weighed amount.

alt: An orange crochet tube still on the hook
caption: Illustration. Even rounds turn the circle into a wall.

alt: A drawstring and a small green stem at the rim
caption: Illustration. The cord uses the eyelets. The stem sits beside them, not in them.

alt: Side view of the pumpkin bag. A flat base of 48 stitches, rounds 9 to 12 straight at 48, round 13 increases to 54, rounds 14 to 21 straight at 54, round 22 decreases to 48, rounds 23 to 28 straight at 48, then the eyelet round 29 and two rounds above it. The belly is about a quarter inch wider on each side.
caption: Six stitches in, six stitches out. The bulge is gentle on purpose so the bag still stands.

alt: Round 13: widen to 54, drawn as rings from the center out. Round 12: undefined, 48 stitches. Round 13: (sc 7, 2 sc in next) 6 times, 54 stitches.
caption: Step 1. Six spaced increases widen the belly from 48 to 54.

alt: Round 22: back to 48, drawn as rings from the center out. Round 21: undefined, 54 stitches. Round 22: (sc 7, sc2tog) 6 times, 48 stitches.
caption: Step 2. Six decreases in the same rhythm take it back to 48 for the neck.

alt: The bag by stitch count, as bars sized by stitch count. Round 1: 6, Round 2: 12, Round 3: 18, Round 4: 24, Round 5: 30, Round 6: 36, Round 7: 42, Round 8: 48, Rounds 9 to 12: 48, Round 13: 54, Rounds 14 to 21: 54, Round 22: 48, Rounds 23 to 28: 48, Round 29: 24+24, Rounds 30 to 31: 48. Round 29 is the eyelet round: 24 sc and 24 chain spaces.
caption: Step 3. The bag by stitch count: flat base, the belly from round 13 to 21, then the neck and the eyelet round.

alt: A small orange crochet pumpkin zipper pouch with a green stem
caption: Illustration. An orange pouch with a stem and a zipper across the top. Not a measured sample.

alt: Orange yarn, green yarn, a hook, and a short zipper
caption: Illustration. Yarn, hook, and zipper. Not a weighed amount of yarn.

alt: A zipper being sewn into the orange pouch
caption: Illustration. Sew the tape to the fabric. Do not crochet into the teeth.

alt: A circular rim of 48 stitches, 12 inches around, and the same rim pinched flat into a 6 inch opening. A 5 inch zipper sits along it with its tape behind the crochet and teeth just below the edge. About half an inch at each end is closed by whipstitching front to back.
caption: Half the circumference is the longest zipper that fits. A little shorter, with the ends closed, sits flatter.

alt: Base: rounds 1 to 8, drawn as rings from the center out. Round 1: 6 sc in a magic ring, 6 stitches. Round 2: 2 sc in each st, 12 stitches. Round 3: (sc, 2 sc in next) 6 times, 18 stitches. Round 4: (sc 2, 2 sc in next) 6 times, 24 stitches. Round 5: (sc 3, 2 sc in next) 6 times, 30 stitches. Round 6: (sc 4, 2 sc in next) 6 times, 36 stitches. Round 7: (sc 5, 2 sc in next) 6 times, 42 stitches. Round 8: (sc 6, 2 sc in next) 6 times, 48 stitches.
caption: Step 1. Round 8 ends on 48 stitches, 12 inches around at 4 sc per inch.

alt: The pouch by stitch count, as bars sized by stitch count. Round 1: 6, Round 2: 12, Round 3: 18, Round 4: 24, Round 5: 30, Round 6: 36, Round 7: 42, Round 8: 48, Rounds 9 to 23: 48. The zipper is sewn behind the top of round 23. Flattened, 48 stitches make a 6 in opening.
caption: Step 2. Fifteen even rounds turn the flat base up into a 3 inch wall.

alt: A soft yarn crochet scrunchie in warm terracotta on a wooden vanity beside a hairbrush
caption: Illustration. A gathered crochet tube on a regular hair elastic. Not a worn sample.

alt: Hands chaining a long foundation for a crochet scrunchie strip
caption: Illustration. The chain is the length of the strip.

alt: A flat crochet rectangle in progress for a hair scrunchie
caption: Illustration. Rows of single crochet until the strip is wide enough.

alt: A tapestry needle seaming a crochet strip into a tube around a hair elastic
caption: Illustration. Fold the long edges together around the elastic and whipstitch closed.

alt: Hands sliding and evening gathers on a finished crochet scrunchie
caption: Illustration. Slide the fabric around until the gathers are even.

alt: An elastic hair tie measuring 7 inches around, beside a crochet strip twice as long, 14 inches, and 2.5 to 3 inches wide. The strip folds lengthwise around the elastic and is seamed along the long edge, then the short ends are joined. At about 5 single crochet rows per inch, 2.5 to 3 inches is 12 to 15 rows.
caption: Length comes from the elastic. Width comes from the rows.

alt: Two rows of single crochet. Correct: the turning ch 1 sits beside the edge and the first sc of the new row goes into the first stitch, the last one made on the row below, so the count stays the same. Mistake: the first sc goes into the ch 1, outside the edge, which adds a stitch and makes the edge flare.
caption: Keeping the count identical means starting each row in the edge stitch, not the ch 1.

alt: Three cross-section steps. 1: lay the elastic along the middle of the strip's wrong side. 2: fold both long edges up over it so they meet. 3: whipstitch the two long edges together along the full length, catching only the crochet and never the elastic, pushing the fabric along as you go because the strip is twice as long as the elastic.
caption: Step 3 in cross-section. The seam closes the fabric around the elastic without piercing it.

alt: A flat five-petal crochet flower in soft pink and yellow on a linen cloth
caption: Illustration. A small flat flower. Not a measured sample.

alt: Hands crocheting a small yellow magic-ring center for a flower
caption: Illustration. Close the ring before the petals. The hands are not a gauge.

alt: A crochet hook forming open petals around a small flower center
caption: Illustration. Each petal is a short group of taller stitches in one center stitch.

alt: A small green crochet leaf beside a finished flower appliqué
caption: Illustration. A tapered strip, not a measured leaf.

alt: A tapestry needle sewing a crochet flower onto fabric
caption: Illustration. Sew the center and the base of each petal.

alt: Diagram of five center stitches, with one petal in each. The petal is chain 2, three double crochet, chain 2, and a slip stitch in that same stitch.
caption: Five centers, five petals. The next petal starts in the next stitch, not in the one you just used.

alt: Diagram of chain 7 with the first chain skipped, then single, half double, double, double, half double, single. Six stitches, one side of the chain only.
caption: The two doubles are the wide part of the strip. There is no second side.

alt: Hands working a white thread snowflake with a fine steel crochet hook
caption: Illustration. The crochet is quick. The blocking decides how it looks.

alt: A finished white crochet snowflake with open stiff points
caption: Illustration. Flat points after stiffening. Not a photographed sample.

alt: A white thread motif with five chain-loop petals radiating from a closed center ring
caption: Illustration. The same construction with five loops instead of six. Nobody would call this a snowflake, which is why the count is the first thing to get right.

alt: A wet white snowflake pinned out flat on a foam blocking board
caption: Illustration. Every point pinned, pulled to full length, and left until bone dry.

alt: A ring of 12 double crochet, six chain-5 loops each using 2 of the 12 stitches, and a picot point in each loop: six arms.
caption: Twelve stitches, six loops, six points. Each round is a multiple of six.

alt: A finished black crochet spider beside a pale gray flat crochet web
caption: Illustration. The intended look. Not a measured sample.

alt: Hands crocheting a small black sphere in the round
caption: Illustration. Each body section is a small ball.

alt: Eight thin black crocheted cords laid out in four matched pairs
caption: Illustration. Eight legs, all the same length.

alt: A tapestry needle stitching two small black eyes onto a crochet spider body
caption: Illustration. Two eyes near the front of the head section.

alt: A pale gray crochet web being worked flat, with the hook still in the work
caption: Illustration. The web is worked flat in rounds of chain loops.

alt: A black crochet spider being sewn slightly off-center onto a pale gray crochet web
caption: Illustration. Off-center looks placed. Dead center looks stamped.

alt: A spider from above with a larger rear body and a smaller front body. All eight legs attach to the front body, four on each side, front pairs angled forward and back pairs angled back, with eyes at the front. A web in rounds: a ring of 8 single crochet, then 8 loops of chain 5, 7, 9, and 11.
caption: Legs belong on the smaller front body. Web loops grow by two chains a round.

alt: Four steps. 1: wrap the yarn around two fingers so the tail crosses over the working yarn. 2: insert the hook under the ring, catch the working yarn, and pull up a loop, then ch 1; the ch 1 is not a stitch. 3: work the stated number of sc into the ring, over both strands of the ring and the tail. 4: pull the tail to close the center, then count the stitches.
caption: Round 1 starts in a magic ring, pulled tight so the top has no hole.

alt: Three steps. 1: insert the hook into the front loop only of the next stitch. 2: without pulling through, insert into the front loop of the stitch after it, so three loops are on the hook. 3: yarn over and pull through the two front loops, then yarn over and pull through the two loops on the hook. Two stitches become one.
caption: Through the front loops only, the decrease disappears into the fabric.

alt: A sage crochet sleeve on a plain handled tumbler
caption: Illustration. The handle stays outside the fabric. Not a tested fit.

alt: Sage cotton, a hook, a button, and a plain tumbler
caption: Illustration. Cotton, a button, and a hook.

alt: The wrap buttoned with the handle outside
caption: Illustration. The handle is not inside the crochet.

alt: A sideways strip 18 stitches tall with a wedge of short rows in the middle. The top edge has 35 plus 4, 39 rows, 7.8 inches; stitches 7 to 12 get 2 extra rows; the bottom edge has 35 rows, 7.0 inches.
